newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guerrillas head for the classroom in Guatemala.
newsitem.headline: Guerrillas head for the classroom in Guatemala.

text.p: Seated primly in class at the National Police Academy, 57 former guerrillas on Wednesday began training to become bodyguards for their former rebel commanders.

The vision of leftist rebels of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) dressed in police academy uniforms has raised eyebrows in Guatemala, where 36 years of civil war pitted state security forces against the insurgents.
But the bodyguards-in-training, who only recently came down from their hiding places in the mountains, said there was nothing strange about the arrangement.

"There were rumours that we would join the National Police, but it's not true. We are receiving this training to serve as security for the URNG high command," former guerrilla Guillermo Figueroa told Reuters.
Figueroa and his classmates are among more than 3,000 ex-combatants of the URNG who are demobilizing, turning in arms, and receiving vocational training before they return to life as normal citizens.

Guerrilla disarmament, as well as reforms in Guatemala's powerful army and police force, are part of the historic peace accords signed on Dec. 29, bringing an end to Central America's last armed conflict.
During the long war, URNG commanders lived in hiding with their fighters in mountain camps or in exile in Mexico.
Guerrilla leaders now live openly and legally in Guatemala and are working to form a legitimate political party. The government has promised them special security.
"In the peace accords we promised to help members of the URNG and to provide them protection when they returned to Guatemala," Deputy Interior Minister Salvador Gandara told Reuters.
Members of the Spanish Civil Guard, who have been leading a variety of training programmes for the Guatemalan National Police, are teaching the security course.
"This is an accelerated one-month class. They wanted a rapid course," Spanish Civil Guard Lt.-Col. Francisco Gabella told Reuters.
Gabella said the classes would include self-defence training and lessons on how to provide protection in vehicles, buildings and on the street.
